claim: Chrysippus accepts premises (1) and (2) but rejects (3) by distinguishing Necessity from that-which-is-necessary
problem: Inverts the ancient report. Epictetus Diss. II.19.1-5 says Diodorus kept (1) 'every past truth is necessary' and (2) 'the impossible does not follow from the possible' and inferred that nothing is possible which neither is nor will be true; Cleanthes rejected (1); Chrysippus kept (1) and (3) 'something is possible which neither is nor will be true' and rejected (2) (δυνατῷ δ' ἀδύνατον ἀκολουθεῖ). The same paragraph also garbles Diodorus: he does not 'abandon' 'nothing is possible that is not or will not be' — that is his conclusion.
correct_proposed: Chrysippus accepts (1) and the possibility of what neither is nor will be true, but rejects (2), holding that the impossible can follow from the possible (Epict. Diss. II.19.1-5).
evidence: Epictetus, Diss. II.19.1-5, Perseus TEI tlg0557.tlg001.perseus-grc2: 'οἱ δὲ τἆλλα δύο, ὅτι δυνατόν τʼ ἐστίν, ὃ οὔτʼ ἔστιν ἀληθὲς οὔτʼ ἔσται, καὶ πᾶν παρεληλυθὸς ἀληθὲς ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστιν, δυνατῷ δʼ ἀδύνατον ἀκολουθεῖ … οἱ δὲ περὶ Χρύσιππον τὰ ἄλλα'
verifier_note: Epict. Diss. II.19.1-5 (cached Perseus TEI) confirms: Chrysippus keeps 'every past truth is necessary' and 'something is possible which neither is nor will be true', and rejects 'the impossible does not follow from the possible'. Proposed text adjusted to fit the node's own numbering, where (3) is Diodorus' conclusion. The same error sits in metadata.description_en and description_fr.
correct_final: Chrysippus accepts premise (1) but rejects (2), holding that the impossible can follow from the possible, and so can maintain that something is possible which neither is nor will be true
replacement: Chrysippus accepts premise (1) but rejects (2), holding that the impossible can follow from the possible, and so can maintain that something is possible which neither is nor will be true

claim: Diodorus abandons (3'), the 'opposed' version (nothing is possible that is not or will not be), in favour of the denial of contingency
problem: Diodorus does not abandon 'nothing is possible which neither is nor will be true'; he uses premises (1) and (2) to establish it (πρὸς παράστασιν τοῦ μηδὲν εἶναι δυνατόν, ὃ οὔτʼ ἔστιν ἀληθὲς οὔτʼ ἔσται). What he rejects is (3), 'something is possible which neither is nor will be true'.
correct_proposed: Diodorus rejects (3), 'something is possible which neither is nor will be true', and concludes that nothing is possible which neither is nor will be true.
evidence: Epictetus, Diss. II.19.1, Perseus TEI tlg0557.tlg001.perseus-grc2

correct_final: Diodorus retains (1) and (2) and rejects the third member of Epictetus' triad, 'something is possible which neither is nor will be true', concluding that nothing is possible which neither is nor will be true

problem: Not in Alexander's De fato. In the treatise ἀξίωμα occurs only in ch. 10, and there in the logical sense of 'proposition' ('τὸ ἀξίωμα τὸ ἔσται αὔριον ναυμαχία'), never 'dignity'. The plural αὐτεξούσιοι does not occur either. Premise 1 and Premise 4 ('physei logikoi kai autexousioi') give invented Greek terminology an Alexandrian source.

claim: (4) These fallen angels introduced fate (εἱμαρμένη) and astrology as demonic deceptions to enslave humans.
problem: Not in 2 Apol. 5-7. There the demons enslave humanity 'partly by magical writings, partly by fears and punishments, partly by teaching sacrifices, incense and libations' (2 Apol. 5). In 2 Apol. 7 Justin says the Stoics, not understanding the demons' activity, wrongly declared that everything happens by the necessity of fate. Justin nowhere makes fate or astrology a demonic invention. That is Tatian's thesis (Orat. 8-9). The 'COROLLARY: fate itself is a demonic invention' is likewise unsupported.
correct_proposed: (4) The demons enslaved humans through magical writings, fears and punishments, and the teaching of sacrifices (2 Apol. 5); the Stoic doctrine of fate is a philosophical error that arose from misunderstanding the demons' activity (2 Apol. 7).
evidence: Justin, 2 Apol. 5 and 7, First1KGreek TEI tlg0645.tlg002.perseus-grc2: 'τὰ μὲν διὰ μαγικῶν γραφῶν, τὰ δὲ διὰ φόβων καὶ τιμωριῶν… τὸ δὲ διὰ διδαχῆς θυμάτων'; 'Ὃ μὴ νοήσαντες οἱ Στωϊκοὶ καθ᾿ εἱμαρμένης ἀνάγκην πάντα γίνεσθαι ἀπεφήναντο'
verifier_note: 2 Apol. 5 (cached TEI): the demons enslaved humanity by magical writings, fears and punishments, and teaching of sacrifices. 2 Apol. 7: 'Ὃ μὴ νοήσαντες οἱ Στωϊκοὶ καθ᾿ εἱμαρμένης ἀνάγκην πάντα γίνεσθαι ἀπεφήναντο'. Justin never makes fate a demonic invention. metadata.premises P4 repeats the error.
correct_final: (4) The demons enslaved humans through magical writings, fears and punishments, and the teaching of sacrifices (2 Apol. 5); the Stoic doctrine of fate is a philosophical error that arose from misunderstanding the demons' activity (2 Apol. 7).
replacement: (4) The demons enslaved humans through magical writings, fears and punishments, and the teaching of sacrifices (2 Apol. 5); the Stoic doctrine of fate is a philosophical error that arose from misunderstanding the demons' activity (2 Apol. 7).

claim: Dial. 88.5 presents moral change as empirical proof of freedom: people who previously lived viciously now choose virtue, which would be impossible under fatalistic determination.
problem: Dial. 88.5 says nothing about moral change. It states that God, wishing angels and humans to be ἐν ἐλευθέρᾳ προαιρέσει καὶ αὐτεξουσίους, made them able to do what each was empowered to do, and will reward or punish them accordingly. The argument from moral change (the same person passing to opposites) is in 1 Apol. 43.

claim: Origen's response: (1) The argos logos is self-refuting — the fatalist who argues for inaction is himself acting; (2) Scripture commands effort, implying its efficacy;
problem: Neither point is Origen's reply in Contra Celsum II.20. There he calls the ἀργὸς λόγος a sophism. He sets out the sick-man form ('if it is fated that you recover, you will recover whether or not you call the doctor') and refutes it by a parallel: if begetting a child is fated, intercourse is still required, so it is false that calling the doctor is 'in vain' when recovery comes by way of medicine. This is the Chrysippean co-fated answer, as the KG's own Bobzien node says. Neither a self-refutation argument nor an appeal to scriptural commands appears.
correct_proposed: Origen's response: (1) the argos logos is a sophism; (2) as with begetting children, which is impossible without intercourse, recovery that comes by way of medicine requires calling the doctor, so it is false that calling the doctor is 'in vain' (the co-fated answer);
evidence: Origen, Contra Celsum II.20, First1KGreek TEI tlg2042.tlg001.perseus-grc1 (Koetschau): '…ὡς γὰρ ἐπὶ τούτου, ἐπεὶ ἀμήχανον καὶ ἀδύνατον τεκνοποιῆσαι τὸν μὴ συνελθόντα γυναικί, οὐ μάτην παραλαμβάνεται τὸ συνελθεῖν γυναικί, οὕτως εἰ τὸ ἀναστῆναι ἐκ τῆς νόσου ὁδῷ τῇ ἀπὸ ἰατρικῆς γίνεται, ἀναγκαίως παραλαμβάνεται ὁ ἰατρός'
verifier_note: CC II.20 (cached First1KGreek TEI): Origen calls the ἀργὸς λόγος a σόφισμα and refutes the sick-man form by the intercourse/begetting parallel. There is no self-refutation argument and no appeal to scriptural commands. Points (3)-(4) of the node may also deserve review.

claim: 'the Greeks had not been previously formulated by the Indian Brahmans or the Jews' (md ll. 6639)
problem: Garbled and misapplied quotation. According to the node's own metadata, Dihle's sentence (ch. I n. 19) reports Megasthenes' claim (FGrH 715 F 3) that no Greek cosmological doctrine had not been formulated earlier by the Brahmans or the Jews. It is about claims of cosmological priority, not about Indian intellectualism in the psychology of action or dharma. Truncated this way, it cannot support the thesis that 'the absence of an autonomous concept of the will is… a structural characteristic of intellectualist cultures (India, Greece, Zoroastrian Iran)'. That attribution to Dihle is not supported by the quoted evidence.
evidence: Node's own metadata.verified_reference: "Dihle 1982, ch. I n.19: 'Megasthenes' statement (FGH 715 F 3) that no cosmological doctrine of the Greeks had not been previously formulated by the Indian Brahmans or the Jews…'"

claim: "totum simul ... spatium comprehendit atque complectitur" (V pr.6) - embracing all things together
problem: Quotation reversed by ellipsis. In Cons. V pr.6 the words are 'Non enim totum simul infinitae licet vitae spatium comprehendit atque complectitur' and describe the WORLD (which, even if everlasting, does NOT embrace its whole life at once and so is not eternal). Cutting 'Non enim' and presenting it as a characterisation of divine aeternitas inverts Boethius' meaning.

claim: Ant. XVIII.13–14 specifies that they hold Fate to determine "most things" while leaving room for human cooperation (συνεργεῖν). Ant. XIII.171–173, the earliest account, reports the same three-way division without further elaboration.

Ant. XVIII.13 says they hold that 'all things are brought about by fate' (πράσσεσθαί τε εἱμαρμένῃ τὰ πάντα) without removing human willing; it neither says 'most things' nor uses συνεργεῖν (the 'fate helps' idea, βοηθεῖν, is BJ II.163).

problem: Chronology reversed. Melito's Peri Pascha is usually dated c. 160-170 and Melito died c. 180, while Ad Autolycum was written after 180 (Book III reckons chronology to the death of Marcus Aurelius). Melito cannot 'echo' Theophilus, and 'first used by Theophilus' ignores that Melito's cognate formula (δεκτικὸς ... ἀγαθοῦ καὶ πονηροῦ) is earlier. claim: In Alexander of Aphrodisias's anti-deterministic metaphysics, human voluntary action involves uncaused motion (κίνησις ἀναίτιος)

claim: Seneca: 'I will do everything as if Fate were watching' - acts fully while accepting fate.
problem: Not a Senecan statement; no such sentence is attested. It appears to distort Ep. 11.8-10, where Seneca relays Epicurus' advice to live 'as if some good man were watching' ('tamquam illo spectante vivamus'), which has nothing to do with fate or reservation. Seneca's actual reservation texts are De beneficiis IV.34.4 ('omnia sapiens cum exceptione facit: si nihil inciderit quod impediat') and De tranquillitate animi 13.2-3, both cited in the node's own metadata.

Ep. 11.8-10 is Epicurus' 'tamquam illo spectante vivamus' about a good man. No 'as if Fate were watching' exists. The translation is aligned with the actual Latin.

claim: Writing c. 200 CE as head of the Peripatetic school in Athens
problem: Overstated. The De fato dedication (Bruns 164) thanks Septimius Severus and Caracalla for his appointment as a teacher of Aristotelian philosophy, without naming a place; 'head of the Peripatetic school' is anachronistic. An Aphrodisias inscription (Chaniotis, AJA 2004) calls him one of the 'diadochoi' at Athens, i.e. holder of an imperial chair. By contrast, the node's 'Phalaris reductio' is textually supported: De fato 19 (Bruns 189-190) says 'no Phalaris is so cruel and senseless' as to punish what happens by nature.

verifier_note: Defensible as is. The Aphrodisias inscription (Chaniotis 2004) calls Alexander 'one of the διάδοχοι at Athens', i.e. holder of the imperially funded Peripatetic chair. 'Diadochos' is the term for a school head, and 'head of the Peripatetic school at Athens' is a common gloss in the literature. The proposed wording is more precise but not needed to remove an error.

claim: How did Chrysippus's cylinder argument respond to Aristotle's critique of determinism, and how does Bobzien reconstruct this exchange?
problem: False presupposition in the flagship example query. No ancient source presents Chrysippus's cylinder (Cicero, De fato 42-43; Gellius, NA 7.2.11) as a response to an Aristotelian critique of determinism, and there is no attested Chrysippus-Aristotle "exchange" for Bobzien to reconstruct. The cylinder answers the objection that if everything happens by fate (antecedent causes), assent and hence praise/blame are not in our power. Cicero, De fato 39, actually lists Aristotle AMONG the necessitarians ("in qua sententia Democritus, Heraclitus, Empedocles, Aristoteles fuit") between whom and the libertarians Chrysippus sought a middle position. Bobzien (Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy, 1998) treats the cylinder as the Stoic reply to the no-responsibility objection, not to Aristotle.
correct_proposed: How did Chrysippus's cylinder analogy answer the objection that universal fate leaves nothing in our power, and how does Bobzien reconstruct his distinction between principal and auxiliary causes?
evidence: Cicero, De fato 39-43 (Müller Teubner 1915, Perseus phi0474.phi054.perseus-lat1, repo corpus passage de281897-..., text quoted verbatim); Gellius NA 7.2.6-11; Bobzien 1998 ch. 6 (expert knowledge for Bobzien).
verifier_note: Checked Cicero Fat. 39-43 in corpus (Müller/Perseus): 39 lists Aristoteles among the necessitarians; 40 gives the dissenters' objection about assent; 41-43 the perfect/auxiliary distinction and cylinder. No Chrysippus-vs-Aristotle exchange exists.
correct_final: How did Chrysippus's cylinder analogy answer the objection that universal fate leaves nothing in our power, and how does Bobzien reconstruct his distinction between principal and auxiliary causes?

claim: How does Chrysippus's cylinder argument respond to Carneades's critique of Stoic determinism, and how does Bobzien reconstruct that exchange?
problem: Anachronistic presupposition in the showcase question: Chrysippus (c. 280-206 BCE) could not respond to Carneades (214/13-129/28 BCE), whose critique of Stoic fate is later and is itself directed against Chrysippus (Cicero, De fato 23, 31-33; Carneades himself said 'if there had been no Chrysippus, I would not exist', Diog. Laert. 4.62). Cicero presents the cylinder (Fat. 42-43) as Chrysippus's answer to the objection that fate removes assent from our power (Fat. 40-41), raised by opponents among the 'old philosophers', not by Carneades. The accompanying badge '150 years apart' (line 627) is also false: their lives overlapped, and their floruits are c. 60-70 years apart.
correct_proposed: How does Chrysippus's cylinder argument answer the objection that fate removes assent from our power, how did Carneades later attack Stoic fate, and how does Bobzien reconstruct the Stoic position?
evidence: Cicero, De fato 23, 31-33, 39-43 (corpus rows phi0474.phi054 sections 39-43); standard dates for Chrysippus and Carneades (Diog. Laert. 7.184 for Chrysippus' death at 73 in Ol. 143; Carneades died 129/8 aged 85, Diog. Laert. 4.65) - expert knowledge for the dates.
verifier_note: Chrysippus d. 208-204 BCE (DL 7.184); Carneades 214/3-129/8 (DL 4.65) wrote against him (DL 4.62). Cicero Fat. 40-43 sets the cylinder against the assent objection. The badges ('2 philosophers' etc.) remain consistent.
correct_final: How does Chrysippus's cylinder argument answer the objection that fate removes assent from our power, how did Carneades later attack Stoic fate, and how does Bobzien reconstruct the Stoic position?

claim: Qualified determinism: some things "depend on us"
problem: Presents the Peripatetic school position on freedom as "qualified determinism". The principal Peripatetic treatment, Alexander of Aphrodisias' De fato, is explicitly anti-determinist (it defends the power to choose and do opposites, De fato 14-15, 19); Aristotle's own stance is contested (Sorabji, Necessity, Cause and Blame 1980, reads him as an indeterminist). Labeling the school "qualified determinism" as fact is at best a contested minority reading and contradicts the project's own gold claims (tests/eval/queries.yaml q008).
correct_proposed: Libertarian/indeterminist (Alexander): what is "up to us" (τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν) is the power to do or not do; Aristotle's own position is debated
evidence: Alexander, De fato 14-15, 19 (corpus rows aed97e25, 6d9d85c8, 4975cde6: αὐτεξούσιον ... κύριον τῆς τῶν ἀντικειμένων αἱρέσεώς τε καὶ πράξεως); Sorabji 1980 (expert knowledge).
verifier_note: Alexander's De fato (corpus ch. 14-15, 19) is explicitly anti-determinist, and Aristotle (De int. 9) rejects universal necessity; 'qualified determinism' is at best a minority reading. The proposed 'Libertarian/indeterminist' imports the modern labels the project elsewhere hedges and is too long for the card. Drop-in keeps the following (τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν).
correct_final: Not everything is necessitated: some things "depend on us"

claim: Alexander of Aphrodisias, De fato, Bruns 185.21
problem: Probable wrong locus for the claim it is attached to. The card says Alexander turns the Stoic image against them ("Give a sphere its nature and a slope, and there is nothing else it could have done. A nature that settles the outcome has explained 'up to us' away"). That polemical use is De fato 36 (the Stoic view makes the agent follow causes "as the stone let go from a height cannot fail to fall, or the sphere released on a slope fail to roll ... what need then of laws?"). At De fato 15 (Bruns 185.21) the sphere occurs in Alexander's own positive definition of human agency, after a lacuna ("τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ εἶναι ἀνθρώπῳ ... ὡς *** τῇ σφαίρᾳ τὸ κατὰ τοῦ πρανοῦς κυλιομένῃ φέρεσθαι"), not as an argument against the Stoics.

evidence: Corpus rows tlg0732_tlg014_grc "De Fato 15" and "De Fato 36" (normalised text quoted above). Sharples 1983 commentary on 185.21 and ch. 36 not checked (expert knowledge).

Chs. 11 (cylinder on a slope) and 19 (round things on a slope) make the same anti-Stoic point. Ch. 15 uses the sphere, after a lacuna, in Alexander's own account of what it is to be a human. claim: Chrysippus's point is that fate operates through the perfect causes
problem: The few-shot exemplar in the synthesis prompt (which every long answer is told to imitate) inverts Chrysippus's doctrine. Cicero, De fato 41 says the opposite: "cum dicimus omnia fato fieri causis antecedentibus, non hoc intellegi volumus: causis perfectis et principalibus, sed causis adiuvantibus et proximis" - fate works through the auxiliary and proximate causes (the external impression), while the perfect/principal cause is the agent's own nature. Line 687-689 tells the model that fate operates through the perfect causes, identified with assent, and 'not ... mediated by auxiliary stimuli'.
correct_proposed: Chrysippus's point is that when everything is said to happen by fate through antecedent causes, the causes meant are the auxiliary and proximate ones (the impression); the perfect and principal cause of assent is the agent's own nature, so assent stays in our power.
evidence: Cicero, De fato 41 (corpus row fc50aff8-32e5-443b-950d-35ad89b15d96, Müller Teubner via Perseus phi0474.phi054.perseus-lat1), text quoted verbatim.

The exemplar inverts this. Applying the drop-in also requires deleting the rest of that sentence (' — the agent's own assent (συγκατάθεσις) — and not as a brute external compulsion mediated by auxiliary stimuli'), keeping ' [P4].'.
correct_final: Chrysippus's point is that the antecedent causes through which fate operates are the auxiliary and proximate ones (the impression), while the perfect and principal cause of assent is the agent's own nature

claim: This solution was broadly endorsed by subsequent ecclesiastical theology (Augustine, Boethius, scholasticism).
problem: Origen's solution in Philocalia 23.8 is that foreknowledge does not cause the future event; rather, the future event is the reason the foreknowledge is what it is. Boethius explicitly rejects this: Cons. V pr. 3 says "Neque enim illam probo rationem qua se quidam credunt hunc quaestionis nodum posse dissoluere. Aiunt enim non ideo quid esse euenturum, quoniam id prouidentia futurum esse prospexerit, sed e contrario potius...". His own answer, the eternity solution in V pr. 4-6, is different. Listing Boethius among those who endorsed Origen's solution is therefore wrong. The sentence also reads as a KG gloss, not a reported view of Amand.
correct_proposed: Hedge the sentence and remove Boethius, e.g. "Later theology took up the principle that foreknowledge is not the cause of what is foreknown (cf. Augustine, DLA III.4.11), although Boethius (Cons. V pr. 3) rejected this solution as insufficient."
evidence: Boethius, Consolatio V pr. 3, Perseus stoa0058.stoa001.perseus-lat2 ("Neque enim illam probo rationem...")
verifier_note: Perseus Cons. V pr.3 has 'Neque enim illam probo rationem ... Aiunt enim non ideo quid esse euenturum, quoniam id prouidentia ... prospexerit, sed e contrario'. DLA III.4.11 has 'sic Deus praescientia sua non cogit facienda quae futura sunt' (mapping.json). The proposed text was not drop-in.
correct_final: This solution was later taken up in various forms (Augustine, for instance, holds that foreknowledge does not compel what it foresees, DLA III.4.11), whereas Boethius (Cons. V pr.3) explicitly rejected the argument that the future event is the cause of the foreknowledge rather than the reverse.
replacement: This solution was later taken up in various forms (Augustine, for instance, holds that foreknowledge does not compel what it foresees, DLA III.4.11), whereas Boethius (Cons. claim: in reality, Gorgias concludes, it is the art of persuasion (λόγος) alone that is culpable, which implies that Helen acted in full freedom.
problem: This misrepresents the Encomium of Helen. Gorgias exculpates Helen under every hypothesis, including persuasion. In §12 persuasion is itself a form of compulsion: "ὁ μὲν οὖν πείσας ὡς ἀναγκάσας ἀδικεῖ, ἡ δὲ πεισθεῖσα ὡς ἀναγκασθεῖσα τῷ λόγῳ μάτην ἀκούει κακῶς". §§15-20 conclude that she is blameless in all four cases. Gorgias does not conclude that Helen 'acted in full freedom'; he argues the opposite.
correct_proposed: Gorgias argues that under each hypothesis (the gods and Necessity, force, persuasion, love) Helen was compelled and is therefore blameless (DK 82 B11 §§6, 12, 15, 20). The persuader bears the guilt, and Helen "being persuaded as one compelled" is wrongly reproached. Amand takes this as the first attestation of the link between compulsion and the injustice of blame.
evidence: Gorgias, Helen (DK 82 B11) §§6, 12, 20. Expert knowledge of the text: no TEI was available in the checked repositories, so the Greek of §12 was not re-verified here.
verifier_note: First1KGreek tlg0593.1st1K001 confirms §12 verbatim, and the conclusion 'πάντως διαφεύγει τὴν αἰτίαν'. The proposed text's last sentence would duplicate the node's following 'Amand identifies here…', so it was trimmed.
correct_final: Gorgias concludes that under every hypothesis, persuasion included, Helen was compelled and is blameless: the persuader, not the persuaded, does wrong (DK 82 B11 §12: ὁ μὲν οὖν πείσας ὡς ἀναγκάσας ἀδικεῖ, ἡ δὲ πεισθεῖσα ὡς ἀναγκασθεῖσα τῷ λόγῳ μάτην ἀκούει κακῶς).
replacement: Gorgias concludes that under every hypothesis, persuasion included, Helen was compelled and is blameless: the persuader, not the persuaded, does wrong (DK 82 B11 §12: ὁ μὲν οὖν πείσας ὡς ἀναγκάσας ἀδικεῖ, ἡ δὲ πεισθεῖσα ὡς ἀναγκασθεῖσα τῷ λόγῳ μάτην ἀκούει κακῶς).
